approach_variants.name: SR-20 pullout, Burgundy Creek climbers' trail, the Bench, Burgundy Col
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the broad pullout and overlook on SR-20 near milepost 165-166, about four miles east of Washington Pass, where a sign points toward Silver Star Mountain.

Drop down the embankment roughly 150 to 200 ft to Early Winters Creek and cross on a log. Logjams shift year to year, so scout up and down for the best crossing and be prepared to ford in high water or early season when the creek runs cold and fast with snowmelt. Treat this crossing as your last reliable water until camp.

On the far bank pick up the unofficial but well-defined climbers' trail that climbs the timbered rib on the west (left) side of the Burgundy Creek drainage. From there it climbs relentlessly and steeply through forest and brush for roughly 2,500-3,000 ft with almost no switchbacks and only fleeting water access early on. The tread erodes and is easy to lose in the timber.
hazards: Early Winters Creek crossing — log can be wet, mossy or washed out; ford in high water
Steep eroding brushy tread that is easy to lose in the timber
Loose microwave-sized blocks in the gully bed above the bench
Loose kitty-litter slabs on the final traverse into the col
No water between the creek and the bench
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The unmistakable break on this approach is the bench, at roughly 6,400-6,700 ft: the grade suddenly eases onto an open larch-and-heather shelf with several established campsites and usually a seasonal trickle or snowmelt nearby. That is the standard overnight camp and the natural turnaround check for a day trip.

Above the bench there is a gully running obviously and directly to Burgundy Col. That gully is the wrong one — it is loose and exposed. Instead stay left and follow the trail up the gully directly above camp. Within it, stay climber's left of the gully proper: the bed holds loose microwave-sized blocks, while the left side is unpleasant kitty-litter-covered slab but far less dangerous. Near the head of the gully make an ascending traverse to the right, under the cliffs, over heather-covered slabs into the col at roughly 7,800 ft. This gully and traverse is where parties describe the real crux of route-finding, both up and down. The col — not the glacier — is where the route proper begins; from there trend toward the northeast side of the west summit.

approach_variants.name: North Fork Entiat to the Pyramid Mountain junction, then the basin between Saska and Emerald
approach_variants.notes:
From the North Fork Entiat River Trailhead near 3,940 ft at the end of FR-5606, take Trail #1437 upstream on a gentle grade — only about 1,300 ft of gain over six miles. The lower miles run through old burn and blowdown, so plan on working over and around deadfall rather than walking clean tread. Grouse Creek has been crossed on a logjam roughly 100 ft upstream of the trail crossing, or on a deteriorating footbridge, depending on the year.

Bear right at the Fern Lake fork and stay on #1437. Around mile 7 the trail swings sharply east and switchbacks half a mile to its end at the Pyramid Mountain Trail junction. In early season the tread gets hard to follow once snow patches start above roughly 4,800 ft.

Leave the maintained trail at the junction and head west; the timber opens into a clearing within about a quarter mile. Fill and treat water there — the valley bottom is the last easy water and there is little of it above.

From the clearing the travel is cross-country: angle west then south-west, contouring below Cardinal Peak's west side toward the basin system south of Emerald. Expect to give back 200-300 ft to skirt cliff bands before regaining the open basin floor around 6,900 ft. A camp flat sits near 7,000-7,100 ft.
approach_variants.season: Mid-Jul-Sep for snow-free scrambling; late May and June need an axe and crampons for neve in the summit gullies. October is popular for larch colour and brings short days
hazards: Loose rock and choss in the summit gullies, with several similar-looking gully and bench variations that do not all go
A small summit area with a steeply inclined south slab whose slip line runs down the east face
Lingering snow and possible cornices in the summit gullies through June
A dry approach above the valley bottom, with the last easy water a quarter mile past the trail's end
Unmaintained, log-choked trail sections from past wildfire damage on the lower six miles
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The start of the climbing is the upper basin wedged between Saska and Emerald, and the thing that leads you into it is running water. From the 6,900 ft basin, cross a shoulder near 7,100 ft and climb a gully system into that upper basin. The slabby watercourse draining it gives the most continuous line and holds snow well into early summer — so in cloud, follow the drainage uphill rather than picking a gully by eye.

The arrival is a bench at about 7,800 ft beneath the south-east side of the summit ridge. From there several scramble lines look much alike and none is obviously better than the rest. That is the honest state of this route and it is why the rule below is a direction rather than a description.

The rule is: work up and to climbers' right to stay on the standard line. Right, from the bench. If you have drifted left you are on one of the variations that this face is full of, and they do not all go.

What the correct gully does at its top, which is the confirmation: it tops out at a notch in the summit ridge, and from that notch it is only a short Class 2-3 scramble to the top — one described account calls it a very short Class 3 scramble near the top. So the test is proportion: if you have topped out of a gully and there is a great deal of climbing still above you, you are in the wrong gully.

The summit is two points about 100 ft apart and the north one is the true, marginally higher top. The south point is a noticeably steeper inclined slab and a slip off it runs down the east face. The whole summit area is small and drops away within a few paces in most directions, and several nearby lower rock points can be mistaken for the summit — so the exposure, not the difficulty, is what deserves attention at the top.

What this route is not: it is not a ridge climb despite the name. The name describes the ridge and notch it gains relative to Cardinal Peak, which sits just to the south-east. The climbing is a gully and a short scramble.

approach_logistics.trailheadDirection: Start at the North Fork Entiat River Trailhead (~3,940 ft) at the end of Forest Road 5606, off Entiat River Road.

approach_variants.name: Smithbrook Trail and the crest trail to Lake Valhalla
approach_variants.notes: From the Smithbrook Trailhead on the gravel spur off the highway, climb the signed Smithbrook Trail through nearly twenty short switchbacks to Union Gap, where it meets the crest trail; the summit is in view to the south for much of that stretch once the forest opens. Turn left and follow the crest trail south, contouring below the mountain's east flank through a mix of forest and open heather meadow and crossing Smith Brook, which is a reliable place to filter before leaving the trail. Where the trail bends away from Lake Valhalla, drop off it down a steep dirt path to the water and follow the rocky shoreline round to the lake's south tip.
approach_variants.season: Snow-free ground roughly July through October; the same slopes are skinned or snowshoed as a separate winter tour. The access road is unplowed in winter and typically melts out by early to mid summer.
hazards: There is no trail of any kind beyond the lake outlet — real tread only reappears on the summit ridge itself
More than one gully runs up this side of the mountain and only one of them is the route
The peak visible from the lake is a lower sub-summit, and parties have climbed it by mistake onto slick class 4 and 5 ground
Short cliff bands that force minor backtracking
Loose talus with rockfall onto anyone below
The gully often holds snow into early summer, so an axe and light traction are worth carrying outside peak summer
approach_variants.baseFinding: When faced with a choice of gullies, take the middle one — and know that the peak you can see is not the summit. From the southeast area of the lake begin a slight ascent to the southeast, looking for the obvious rock-filled gully. Be careful here: there is more than one gully on this side of the mountain, and the middle of them is the route. Ascend it to where it terminates, then work around the first small cliff band to the left, on its north side. Above that, climb right toward a gentle saddle; from the saddle a traverse northeast is the easier finish, while going northwest is the exposed option and is not the ordinary line. The wrong-place marker is the thing you have been looking at all along: from the lake the true summit is hidden, and what stands in front of it is a smaller unnamed peak that looks steep and sketchy. Parties have climbed toward it by mistake and turned back a few metres short on slick class 4 and 5 rock. There is no trail at all beyond the lake outlet, so finding none is expected; real tread reappears only on the summit ridge.

approach_variants.name: Middle Fork Nooksack Road (FR-38) and Rankin Creek to the treeline camp, then the southwest basin
approach_variants.notes:
This is the more direct way to the X Couloir: from the south via the Middle Fork Nooksack River Road (FR-38). The southwest face can also be reached from Heliotrope Ridge through the Thunder Glacier cirque, a less direct line with more glacier travel; do not confuse either with the north-facing Coleman side, which leads to the other route on this mountain.

Drive FR-38 toward its mile-12.5 switchback and start walking the old decommissioned road around Point 4481 toward Rankin Creek. Snow travel — often by bike or snowshoe on the lower stretch — leads past East Rankin Lake near 5,120 ft and up into the basin to a sheltered camp at treeline around 6,100 ft, by the highest trees in the basin below Seward Peak. Roughly seven miles and 3,350 ft of gain to camp.

Access: FR-38, damaged in the December 2025 floods, has been closed to vehicles at milepost 7 by a washout since July 27, 2026, with no end date given on the Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest alert still posted on September 26, 2026, and a separate gate at Wallace Creek near mile 10 closes the road 1 December to 15 June for elk calving. Confirm the drivable road-end with the Mount Baker Ranger District before the trip; the length of the approach varies year to year.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Apr-Jun. A spring snow climb; essentially never done in summer, because what makes it climbable is continuous snow rather than the rubble underneath
hazards: A bergschrund crossing that must be done cold and early
1,500 ft of 30-40 degree snow with a steep serac step, all of it above a long runout
FR-38 flood damage with no repair timeline, plus an elk-calving gate closed 1 Dec - 15 Jun
A gully that funnels rockfall and spindrift after storms
A descent that is a real rappel sequence off pickets and slung horns, not a walk-off
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The highest trees in the basin are the camp, and the camp is the last thing you can navigate to. Above treeline the southwest side of Lincoln is open snow and there is nothing to hold on to in cloud. So the arrival marker is vegetative rather than topographic: climb until the trees stop, and camp at the last of them, below Seward Peak, around 6,100 ft.

The bergschrund is the base of the climb. From camp an alpine start takes you into the southwest basin and to the schrund while the snow is still cold and firm. Above it is roughly 1,500 ft of 30-40 degree snow with a steep serac step in it.

Do not expect one clean couloir — this is the trap the name sets. Parties who have climbed and skied it describe it as less a couloir and more a series of steep chutes and faces, and the line drops from the high point to the highest notch, then down a narrow chute, and trends right out of view. So 'find the obvious couloir' is the wrong instruction and will have you standing in the basin looking for something that is not there. Work from the notch downward: the correct line is the one that connects to the highest notch on the skyline, and it is narrow where it leaves the basin.

The serac step is the confirmation. Somewhere in that 1,500 ft you meet a steep serac step. A line with no ice step in it is not the X Couloir.

And the aspect settles the coarse error: this route faces southwest and this approach reaches it from Rankin Creek. If you are standing on the Coleman Glacier looking at a shaded north-facing cirque, you are under the other route on this mountain.

approach_variants.name: Trail #1587 from US-2 to the Nason Ridge crest
approach_variants.notes: One of the steepest maintained trails near Stevens Pass, and it starts working immediately. From the dirt pullout on the north side of the highway the tread climbs on an old service road beneath powerlines, leaves the roadbed at a signed bend about a third of a mile up, and then runs into ninety-odd tight switchbacks on an open south-facing slope with no shade at all. Schilling Creek near the bottom is the only accessible water on the climb and it drops away quickly, so fill everything at the car and carry three litres or more. The grade eases into heather meadows around 2.8 miles and the tread tops out on the crest at about 6,000 ft. An alternate approach comes up the Snowy Creek trail from the Smithbrook road and joins the ridge higher.
approach_variants.season: Late June to October; snow lingers
hazards: No reliable water on route above the creek low down
Fully exposed south-facing switchbacks with real heat and sun load
Loose rock and jumbled talus on the upper ridge
A north-facing snow patch below the summit ridge can persist into fall and goes slick by afternoon
A cornice or residual snow on the narrow connecting ridge into early summer
Afternoon thunderstorms on a wholly exposed crest
Habituated mountain goats near the summit — keep your distance
approach_variants.baseFinding: Two signed junctions bracket the start of the scrambling and neither is the base by itself. The first is where the trail tops out on the crest at roughly 6,000 ft and meets the Nason Ridge trail; turn left along the ridge here, since the right-hand branch drops away toward a lake overlook. The second, about half a mile on, is where the Snowy Creek trail joins from the south — that is the alternate approach, not your line, and past it the constructed tread stops being tread and thins into a path over loose jumbled talus. That change underfoot is the base. From there the crest runs over a false south summit first; it carries no structure on it. The true summit beyond is identified by the stone foundation of the old fire lookout, and the short connecting ridge between the two is narrow enough to want care and can hold a cornice or old snow into early summer. If you are standing on a high point with nothing built on it and the ridge carries on, keep going.

approach_logistics.trailheadDirection: From the Rock Mountain Trail #1587 pullout on US-2 (small dirt lot on the north side of the highway near the powerlines, no facilities), the trail launches immediately uphill on what was formerly a service road.
From the Old Lake Valhalla/Lake Janus Trailhead on Smith Brook Road (~4,150 ft)

approach_variants.name: Fryingpan Creek, Summerland and Meany Crest to Whitman Notch
approach_variants.notes:
Start at the Fryingpan Creek Trailhead near 3,800-3,900 ft on the Sunrise and White River Road, a few miles past the White River entrance station. Follow the signed trail up through old-growth beside Fryingpan Creek.

At roughly 3.2 miles and about 1,400 ft of gain there is an established footlog crossing of Fryingpan Creek — the main water and a spot that needs care in high runoff. Continue to Summerland at about 4.5 miles and roughly 5,900 ft: patrol cabin, pit toilet, bear wires, and the last reliable running water.

From Summerland leave maintained trail and take the climbers' path northwest of the campground knoll, up steep tundra and snow on the Meany Snowfield to Meany Crest, a rock outcrop at roughly 7,350-7,500 ft with flat sites and stone wind breaks. This is the standard high camp.

Above Meany Crest gain the toe of the Fryingpan Glacier and rope up. Climb south and southwest across the lower apron to the broad notch between the Fryingpan and Whitman glaciers at about 9,000-9,100 ft, then traverse and climb the upper Whitman across a bergschrund to about 10,500-11,000 ft, where snow gives way to rock.

The basin holds heavy snow and the approach slopes can be avalanche terrain in soft early-season conditions. Afternoon whiteout and thunderstorm activity is common on Rainier's flanks.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun through Aug, best early July to early August — firm morning snow, drier rock, and bridges not yet melted out
hazards: Loose volcanic rock and rockfall on the summit gully and crest, worsening through the day
Crevasses and weakening bridges on the Fryingpan and Whitman glaciers, worst in August and September
A bergschrund that is a step-across early season and a problem late
Cliff-out potential between Summerland and Meany Crest if the line drifts climber's right
Avalanche potential on the Meany Snowfield in soft or early-season conditions
Major exposure on the final crest, with about 2,000 ft to the Emmons on the north side
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Whitman Notch at about 9,100 ft is the arrival, and you know it by what becomes visible rather than by the altimeter: it is the first place the Whitman Glacier comes into view. Until you can see a second glacier on the far side, you have not reached the notch.

The base of the climbing proper is higher still, and it is a change of surface: at about 10,500-11,000 ft the snow ends and a loose rock-and-scree gully begins. That transition is the base. The sequence above it is countable and in this order: gully, a short step of about 6 ft, a gully-chimney, the summit notch, then an exposed scramble along the crest.

The route-finding trap is low, not high, and it is the one thing on this climb that regularly commits parties to bad ground: between Summerland and Meany Crest, if you find yourself contouring climber's right into a bowl under rock bands, you are cliffed out and off the line. The cairned and boot-packed line stays left of that bowl. Fix this by going back to the last cairn, not by traversing further.

The summit-crest test is a negative and it is unambiguous: the last 30 to 100 ft is a narrow crumbling andesite crest with roughly 2,000 ft dropping away to the Emmons Glacier on the north side. If the ground is not falling away on both sides of you, you have not reached the true summit — you are on the notch or a subsidiary block below it.

Timing as a finding: the andesite loosens as the sun works on it, and the crevasse bridges soften through the day. Being at the notch early is not tidiness, it is the whole plan.
